hinweis: Versioned research from project recordings and archived public sources. Each study names its actual observation window, method and limitations. Paper fills, marked inventory and quoted prices are not realised account returns.
einleitung: Recent September and October studies examine execution latency, market-making queues, source speed, arbitrage validation and paired forecasts. Historical studies retain their original samples and now name the next question to test. Page export dates do not extend an observation window. Planned follow-ups are proposals, not new results.

studien.frage: Does book imbalance predict which way the price moves?
studien.verdikt: In this historical sample: 55.5% directional hit rate at five minutes, with a descriptive Wilson lower bound of 55.2%.

analyse.text: How often the mid price, five minutes later, had moved in the direction the order book was leaning.

Each recorded snapshot is checked for an imbalance past a fixed threshold. When it fires, the side it leans to is written down, and compared against where the mid actually sat 300 seconds later, with no decision delay between the firing and the entry price. Firings where nothing moved at all are counted separately so they cannot pad the score. The study also runs four other horizon and delay cells; they are reported in the table below, never pooled, because every snapshot feeds each of them.
Order books this project recorded itself on a 120 second grid, both venues, across eleven days.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: The original Wilson threshold treats firings as independent. A generalisable signal now requires uncertainty clustered by day and event, followed by a locked test on fresh events. The historical hit rate alone does not settle that question.

studien.einfach: Out of 205,835 firings the book pointed the right way 55.5 percent of the time, against the 50 percent a coin flip would give. Even the cautious end of the interval sits at 55.2 percent under the interval's independence assumption. Repeated and overlapping observations limit that assumption. In 35.4 percent of firings the price actually moved at all; the rest sat still.

interpretation.text: Book imbalance aligns with the direction of later moves in this sample. Clustered uncertainty and fresh events are needed to test how reliably that association generalises.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: A hit rate says nothing about size. Being right often on tiny moves and wrong occasionally on large ones produces exactly this number and still loses money. That is the next study.

The grid is 120 seconds and repeated firings share markets and events. The Wilson interval treats trials as independent; it is descriptive here and does not replace day- or event-clustered uncertainty. Faster data and new events are separate tests.

follow_up.question: Does a frozen imbalance rule improve prediction on new events after latency, with uncertainty clustered by day and event?

studien.frage: Can that signal be taken as a taker?
studien.verdikt: No. The edge is worth +0.09 cents per firing against a 2.58 cent round trip.

analyse.text: What is left per firing after the two costs a taker cannot avoid: crossing the spread, and the venue fee.

For each firing the price move is converted to cents per share. Then half the spread standing in the book at decision time is subtracted, and the fee schedule for that market's category on top. What remains is the net.
The same eleven days (2026-07-18 to 07-28) and the same 205,835 firings as study 1, book imbalance, so the two are directly comparable.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: Takeable means the net stays above zero. Costs come from the venue fee model in the repository, not from a round-number assumption. The rate that model is fed is the one input that is not settled: the venue documentation puts the general taker rate at 5 percent and secondary sources from the same period at 3 percent, so every fee figure is carried across both.

studien.einfach: The signal is worth +0.09 cents per firing before costs. Crossing the spread costs 0.938 cents and the venue fee another 1.646, so the round trip takes 2.58 cents, roughly 30 times what the signal produces. The net is -2.50 cents, and only 3.8 percent of firings end positive. The fee rate is disputed; at the lower published rate the fee falls to 0.988 cents and the net only improves to -1.84, still 22 times the signal. Even the best cut of the signal only reaches +0.21 cents gross, nowhere near the wall.

interpretation.text: Being right and making money are different questions, and this is the gap between them. Any analysis that stops at a hit rate has stopped one step too early.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: This only condemns taking. A market maker does not pay the spread, they earn it, so the same information could still be worth something from the other side of the book. That is why the market-making studies follow.

It assumes taking at the touch. A patient limit order would pay less, but then the fill is no longer certain, and an unfilled order earns nothing at all. And the fee rate is not settled: documentation and secondary sources disagree by a factor that moves every fee figure here by 40 percent. The verdict survives both ends, but a narrower gross edge would not have.

follow_up.question: Does the same rule retain executable net value after category-specific fees, available depth, entry and exit latency, and capital use?

studien.frage: Is signed order flow a usable signal?
studien.verdikt: No. 51.7% hit rate at the same five-minute, no-delay cell (Wilson lower bound 51.3%), and the gross edge is negative before any cost.

analyse.text: The same forward hit rate as the imbalance study, but for a signal built out of trade direction rather than resting orders.

Each print on the tape is labelled a buy or a sell by comparing its price against the quote at the time. Those labels are summed into a signed volume imbalance, and that is checked forward exactly like the book signal.
The same recorded tape and the same eleven days as studies 1 and 2, so the difference is the signal and not the sample.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: The identical Wilson bar as the first study. Holding the test fixed is the whole point of running it on the same data.

studien.einfach: Over 93,868 firings this signal was right 51.7 percent of the time, barely above the coin flip and far below the 55.5 percent the resting book managed. Its gross edge is -0.002 cents, already negative before a single cost is subtracted, which means there is nothing here for costs to eat.

interpretation.text: The weak link is the labelling step, not the idea. Order flow ought to be informative, but you have to know which side actually initiated, and here that has to be guessed.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: Published work later found that trade-direction inference on this venue lands between 49.8 and 50.5 percent depending on method. On that reading this measures the method, not the market, and the market question stays open.
Only one inference rule was tested. A venue that published true aggressor flags could give a different answer, and this study cannot rule that out.

follow_up.question: Does independently validated aggressor labelling add predictive value on new events after accounting for trade-clock and coverage errors?

studien.frage: Does any segment of the market rescue the signal?
studien.verdikt: No. One cut survives out of many, which is what pure chance predicts.

analyse.text: The net result per firing inside each slice of the market, to see whether the cost wall has a gap somewhere.

The firings are cut three ways: by the spread standing in the book, by the price level, and by how strongly the signal fired. Every bucket was fixed before looking at any result, and each one is evaluated separately in sample, out of sample, and with a day-resampled confidence interval.
205,835 firings over eleven days, run through three different fee scenarios because the fee depends on the market category.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: A slice counts only if it holds up in sample and out of sample and its interval excludes zero. Two out of three would not do, because with this many tests two out of three happens by luck.

studien.einfach: 34 cuts were tested in each of 3 fee scenarios, 102 tests in total, and 1 survived. That is not encouraging, it is expected: run this many tests on noise and roughly one will look good anyway. The survivor nets +0.008 cents, and its interval [-0.112, +0.203] contains zero, so it is not distinguishable from luck. Across all firings the net stays at -2.50 cents.

interpretation.text: There is no hiding place. The cost wall stands in wide spreads and narrow ones, at long odds and short, on strong signals and weak.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: One survivor could in principle be a real but thin effect that this sample is too small to confirm. The honest way to settle that is fresh data, not a louder claim about the same data.
Only cuts that are knowable before the trade were allowed. A cut using information available afterwards would look far better and would mean nothing at all.

studien.frage: Does market making carry at a 120 second requote?
studien.verdikt: No. Adverse selection takes 362 cents per fill against 148 cents of spread earned, in the tape fill model.

analyse.text: Profit per fill, split into the spread earned by quoting and the amount the market takes back immediately afterwards.

Quotes are placed either side of the mid at a fixed half spread and refreshed every 120 seconds. Each fill is then marked out against the mid a short time later. The difference between what the quote earned and where the price went is the adverse selection.
Recorded books over twelve days and 4,519 tokens, replayed offline. No orders were ever sent.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: Carrying means the net per fill stays above zero once adverse selection is counted. Total profit alone would not do, because quoting less can raise it while the per-fill economics stay broken.

studien.einfach: Each fill earns 148 cents of spread and hands back 362 cents almost immediately, leaving -338 cents. The reason is who trades against a stale quote: whoever already knows the price has moved. Over 13,341 fills across 12 days that pattern does not average out, it is the pattern.

interpretation.text: The problem is adverse selection, not fees. Being picked off costs more than twice what the spread pays, so no fee rebate would fix it.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: It could be the parameters rather than the idea. A wider half spread or stronger inventory aversion might change the balance, and sweeps over both are in the full report.
120 seconds is very slow for quoting. This result may say more about the refresh rate than about market making, which is exactly what the next study tests.

follow_up.question: Can a continuously financed portfolio earn positive conservative exit PnL after partial fills, queue position, quote and cancellation latency?

studien.frage: Is the binding constraint spread width or quote staleness?
studien.verdikt: Consistent with staleness: on seconds data the loss per fill falls from 362 to 70 cents while the spread earned barely moves.

analyse.text: The same two quantities as study 5 (market making at a 120-second requote), spread earned and adverse selection, recomputed on seconds-resolution data.

Identical code, identical parameters, identical fill model. What differs is how fresh the book is when the quote is placed. It is not a controlled experiment: the two runs also cover different days and a different set of tokens, so the data frequency is the main difference rather than the only one.
5,413,998 streamed snapshots over five days and 468 tokens from the WebSocket recorders, against twelve days and 4,519 tokens on the 120 second grid. The two windows do not overlap.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: Lower markout loss with similar spread earned is evidence consistent with staleness. Different days and market universes prevent this comparison from isolating a causal effect of recording frequency.

studien.einfach: Adverse selection falls from 362 cents per fill to 70, which is 81 percent of the loss gone. Meanwhile the spread earned barely moves, from 148 to 138 cents. This pattern is consistent with stale quotes contributing to losses. Different days, markets and fill composition remain alternative explanations; this comparison does not isolate the cause.

interpretation.text: The pattern supports testing quote freshness directly. A matched latency sweep on the same events can distinguish an execution effect from a change in the market sample.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: The two runs are not perfectly matched. Seconds data also produces a different set of fills, across different moments and a shorter window, so part of the improvement could be the changed mix rather than the freshness.
Even at seconds resolution there is still no queue position, so this says the loss shrinks, not that the strategy pays. The next study is about exactly that gap.

studien.frage: Does market making pay, once the bootstrap can run?
studien.verdikt: Not identified. Two fill models land on opposite sides of zero and neither interval touches it.

analyse.text: Daily profit with a confidence interval, computed twice under two different assumptions about when a quote would have been filled.

The touch model assumes a fill whenever the price reaches the quote. The tape model assumes a fill only when a real print happened there. Daily totals are then resampled in blocks so the interval respects that days are not independent of themselves.
The same five days of seconds data as study 6 (468 tokens, 5,413,998 snapshots), both fill models run over identical quotes.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: Identified means both models agree on the sign. If they disagree, the answer depends on the assumption rather than on the data, and no result can honestly be claimed.

studien.einfach: Assume a fill whenever the price touches the quote and the answer is a loss between -12,121 and -2,413 dollars a day. Assume a fill only against a print that really happened and it is a profit between 881 and 5,889. Both intervals sit well clear of zero, in opposite directions. The difference is not noise, it is the assumption, and the assumption cannot be checked from outside the exchange.

interpretation.text: Profitability is unresolved. The two fill models produce conflicting scenario results; neither measures actual own-order execution.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: Actual results need not lie between these scenarios. Queue priority, partial fills, cancels, funding and exit timing can change both the fill set and its economics.
More days would not settle this. It is an identification problem, not a sample size problem, and only order-level queue data would resolve it.

follow_up.question: Do conservative queue and execution scenarios agree on net portfolio PnL in prospective event holdouts with capital and inventory carried forward?

studien.frage: Are price gaps between the two venues arbitrage?
studien.verdikt: Executable arbitrage is not established. Surviving quoted gaps settle in 2027 or 2028, worth 0.5 to 1.8 percent annualised under the stated assumptions.

analyse.text: The net gap per share between the two venues on the same event, after both fee curves, and what that is worth per year.

Markets are matched by what the question actually asks rather than by wording overlap. For each surviving pair both books are priced, each venue's own fee curve is subtracted, and the remainder is annualised over the days until settlement.
300 Polymarket markets against 600 Kalshi markets, matched down to a handful of confirmed pairs.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: A quoted gap is a candidate. Executable arbitrage additionally requires equivalent settlement, simultaneously available depth for both legs and a positive result after fees, execution risk and the opportunity cost of committed capital.

studien.einfach: 300 markets on one venue were matched against 600 on the other, giving 8 pairs. 3 were thrown out as mismatched questions, leaving 5 usable, of which 3 clear both fee curves. The best is 3.07 cents per share. But those all settle in 2027 or 2028, so the money is locked up for years and the return per year is tiny.

interpretation.text: Long settlement horizons make capital commitment central to the result. The measured gaps are consistent with carry, but this snapshot does not establish their economic cause or an executable profit.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: A small annualised quoted return may or may not cover financing and settlement risk. The answer depends on available capital, equivalent payouts and executable size, which this snapshot does not jointly measure.
Three of the eight pairs were rejected as mismatched. The matcher is the weak point of this study, which is why the rejected pairs stay in the table instead of being quietly dropped.

follow_up.question: Which rule-equivalent pairs retain executable net value at simultaneous depth after both fees, leg risk, financing and settlement?

studien.frage: How long does such a gap stay open?
studien.verdikt: Most stayed open at every single moment observed.

analyse.text: The share of observed time each gap was actually open, meaning both legs cleared their fee curve at the same moment.

Both stream recorders cover the same pairs over one window. At paired recorded observations the two books are compared and the gap is marked open or closed. Gaps in coverage cannot establish continuous availability.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: Report persistence within joint recorded coverage. Persistence alone does not identify a fair price, the reason for a gap or whether both legs could have been executed throughout the interval.

studien.einfach: Of 5 pairs watched over 11.6 hours, 3 were open at every single moment observed and 1 never opened at all. Nothing in between converged. This describes the recorded observations. It does not prove continuous execution availability or explain why the gaps persisted.

interpretation.text: Persistent quoted gaps are consistent with capital commitment and settlement risk. The observations do not identify those mechanisms causally or prove that the quotes represent fair value.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: Eleven hours is a short window. A gap that closes weekly would look permanently open here, and this study could not tell the difference.
Five pairs is a very small sample. This supports the carry reading of study 8 (cross-venue gaps) rather than standing on its own.

studien.frage: Are the large liquidity reward pools free money?
studien.verdikt: No. Many of the biggest pools have a completely empty qualifying band.

analyse.text: Whether anybody is quoting inside the narrow band a reward actually requires, in the markets paying the largest pools.
Every market carrying a pool is ranked by daily payout. For the largest, the live book is probed against the band the reward demands, and the quotes actually standing there are counted.
9,900 markets carrying a pool, together paying out over 164,000 dollars a day, with the 45 largest probed in detail.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: Free money would mean a large pool with a reachable band. A pool nobody can qualify for is not an opportunity, however large the number looks.

studien.einfach: 9,900 markets carry a reward pool, paying out $164,661 a day between them. Of the 45 largest, 14 have a qualifying band with nothing in it at all, which is 31 percent. The quotes that do exist sit far outside the band the reward needs. The pool is large because it is unreachable, not despite it.

interpretation.text: Pool size is not opportunity size. The headline number measures what nobody has collected, which is the opposite of what it looks like.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: An empty band is also an open invitation, if you can quote there and survive. What surviving costs is exactly what the market-making studies measure, and that answer was not encouraging.
This is one snapshot on one date. Bands empty and fill over time, and a different day could look different.

studien.frage: Do two venues settle the same event the same way?
studien.verdikt: No. One asks who is inaugurated, the other who wins the election.

analyse.text: Whether a matched pair of markets settles on the same underlying fact, read from each venue's own settlement text.
Both rulebooks are put side by side and the conditions compared. Where one side carries a condition the other does not, that is flagged, because that is precisely where a hedge stops hedging.
Five confirmed pairs, with both venues' settlement texts read in full rather than skimmed from titles.

analyse.titel: What would have counted as a yes
analyse.text: Same wording is not the test. The test is whether the same real-world outcome pays out on both sides.

studien.einfach: 5 confirmed pairs were checked, 5 with both settlement texts available, and 5 settle on a different fact than they appear to. One venue pays on who is next inaugurated, the other on who wins the election. Those are usually the same person and occasionally not, and the occasionally is the whole risk.

interpretation.text: Matching by title is not enough. This is the trap sitting underneath every cross-venue trade, and it only shows up when it costs you both legs at once.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: For most pairs the wording does agree. This is a per-pair risk to be read before trading, not a reason to write off cross-venue work altogether.
The reading is manual and the sample is five pairs. It proves the failure mode exists, not how common it is.

studien.frage: Does a CEX impulse survive execution delay in a fresh paper window?
studien.verdikt: Open. The 250 ms replay is positive, but 500 ms and 1,000 ms replays are negative under assumed execution delays.

analyse.text: The unchanged CEX lead and lag paper rule was replayed across completed hourly blocks at several assumed entry delays.
Each block and variant restarts with 100 USD and 10 shares. Closed-trade net includes fees; the floor subtracts open-entry costs.
The frozen forward snapshot covers 21 full hourly blocks and 46 time-separated qualifying impulses.
A practical yes needs independently measured order and fill timing and a further untouched window that survives those delays and open-position risk.

studien.einfach: Across 21 hourly blocks and 46 qualifying impulses, the 250 ms baseline closed 193 trades for +32.27 USD net. Its open-position loss floor is +30.62 USD. At 500 and 1,000 ms, closed-trade net falls to -9.72 and -29.25 USD. These are separate paper scenarios, not one portfolio.

interpretation.text: The sign change across the assumed delays makes execution speed central to this signal's practical value.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: The positive 250 ms sum can still reflect optimistic fill assumptions and an unusually favourable short market window.
No real order or fill times were observed, and open positions can change the eventual result after this snapshot.

studien.frage: What happens when both entry and exit are delayed?
studien.verdikt: Open. The six-block baseline changes from positive at 350/350 ms to negative at 500/500 and 1,000/1,000 ms.

analyse.text: A separate sensitivity replay delayed both the simulated entry and the intended exit of the existing CEX rules.
The original six completed hours were replayed with fixed 350/350, 500/500 and 1,000/1,000 ms scenarios; rules and budgets stayed fixed.
These 6 hours were already seen, and the unchanged 250 ms arm had only 23 qualifying impulses.
An independent test with measured order and fill times, enough qualifying impulses and accounted open positions would be needed for a practical claim.

studien.einfach: With entry and exit each delayed 350 ms, the baseline earned +5.18 USD on closed trades across six blocks. At 500/500 ms it returned -5.54 USD; at 1,000/1,000 ms it returned -16.08 USD. All three are assumptions on previously seen data, with separate 100 USD resets per block.

interpretation.text: Adding exit latency can erase a paper advantage even when the entry rule and recorded books are unchanged.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: Different delays also alter which later signals remain executable, so the change is not solely the exit price of identical trades.
Fixed delays are not measured order times; the six reused hours and open positions do not establish live profitability.

studien.frage: Does the market-making quote rule survive queue and refresh delay in the September test window?
studien.verdikt: No for practical execution: the registered zero-delay simulation is positive, while both 250 ms queue scenarios are strongly negative.

analyse.text: A frozen quote rule was tested on fourteen days under queue-front and queue-back fill models, with zero and 250 ms refresh delay.
The original market-making study simulated daily inventories and reported sums, fill counts and bootstrap intervals for the daily mean.
The 14 dates from the separate market-making project include a 29.746-hour recording gap.
The zero-delay primary threshold was met internally, but a practical yes would require funded limits and verified latency, queue position and fills.

studien.einfach: In the conservative queue-back model, zero delay gave +36794.77 USD over 20385 simulated fills. At 250 ms, it gave -39705.31 USD over 33658 simulated fills. The front-of-queue model also flips sign. These are model sums with daily inventory resets and no shared capital budget, not account returns.

interpretation.text: The large sign reversal is consistent with stale quotes being selected after the market moves.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: The zero-delay result may be inflated by unverified queue priority, assumed rebates and marking leftover inventory at the mid.
A 29.746-hour data gap and no hard portfolio budget limit prevent treating the sums as an executable return.

studien.frage: Did faster ISW or DeepState detection reveal a tradeable information edge?
studien.verdikt: No verified speed edge. One Bilytske quote was tiny, and the 100 USD depth simulation was negative.

analyse.text: The source study compared detection times, public trades and recorded bid-ask depth for matched Ukraine event markets.
Historical books were aligned with each signal and later trades; a size-aware 100 USD entry and observed exit were simulated.
Of 39 event-market rows, 20 had a usable book at detection between late September and 11 October.
A yes needs repeated qualifying market events, depth for realistic size and observed fills before a later public reaction.

studien.einfach: The Bilytske source was detected 2836 seconds before a related Telegram post, but its best ask showed only 5 shares costing 2.70 USD. A 100 USD depth-aware entry would have returned -4.51 USD after 24 hours. Only 20 of 39 event-market rows had a usable initial book.

interpretation.text: A faster source timestamp did not translate into enough displayed depth for the tested 100 USD size.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: The later buy could have unrelated causes, and the same small ask had appeared earlier; timing alone does not prove causation.
Displayed book depth is not an own fill, and an event matched by place name may fail the market's actual resolution rule.

studien.frage: How many raw arbitrage scans survived validation and reached paper trading?
studien.verdikt: No validated opportunity reached paper trading in this 24-hour scan window.

analyse.text: A daily bot report counted scan cycles, raw scanner candidates, validation outcomes and paper fires for three arbitrage families.
The scanner's raw counts were compared with its validated and paper stages; counts are repeated scan occurrences, not independent trades.
The 24-hour report records 278 successful cycles of 335 attempted, with 57 failed cycles.
A tradeable claim would require a validated, rules-equivalent candidate, executable quotes and a controlled paper fill before any PnL statement.

studien.einfach: The bot completed 278 of 335 scan cycles; 57 failed. It saw 2505 raw cross-venue, 838 raw negative-risk and 23 raw within-market candidates. Zero passed validation and zero became a paper trade. These are repeated scan counts, not separate available opportunities or realised profit.

interpretation.text: The validation funnel rejected every raw candidate, so the observed scan output does not support an executable arbitrage claim.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: The high raw count can mostly reflect repeated quotes and rule mismatches; it is not a count of unique chances.
Failed scan cycles limit coverage, and forward quote replay does not establish realised PnL or actual fills.

studien.frage: Did Polymarket or FedWatch forecast FOMC decisions more accurately at fixed horizons?
studien.verdikt: Open. The lower Brier score switches by horizon across only five meetings, so there is no overall winner.

analyse.text: Polymarket and archived FedWatch probability distributions were compared with the realised FOMC decision at three fixed horizons.
For each meeting and horizon, the published comparison calculates multiclass Brier scores from the stored probabilities.
The checked-in dataset contains 5 meetings, from 18 March through 16 September 2026.
A broad ranking needs more settled meetings and aligned observation times and execution-aware market prices across horizons.

studien.einfach: Across 5 meetings, mean Brier scores at T-30 were 0.241 for Polymarket and 0.217 for FedWatch. At T-7 they were 0.096 and 0.092; at T-1, 0.037 and 0.055. Lower is better, and the ordering changes with the horizon.

interpretation.text: FedWatch scores lower at the earlier horizons in this sample, while Polymarket scores lower one day before the decision.

interpretation.titel: What else fits the same numbers
interpretation.text: A single September rate hike and different timestamp conventions can materially shift a five-meeting average.
Polymarket observations are hourly market prices rather than executable bid-ask quotes, and five meetings cannot settle a general ranking.
